Speculative decoding is a technique designed to accelerate text generation by leveraging the fact that large language models are often deterministic in their predictions. The core idea is to introduce a smaller, faster "draft" model to propose a sequence of tokens, which a larger, more accurate "target" model then verifies.

The process begins with the draft model generating a short sequence of tokens, such as five words, in parallel. This is significantly faster than the target model generating those same tokens one by one. The target model then evaluates this entire proposed sequence at once. If the target model agrees with the draft model’s prediction for all tokens in the sequence, the entire block is accepted, and the process repeats. This effectively allows the system to generate multiple tokens in a single forward pass of the slower model, rather than waiting for each token to be generated sequentially.

If the target model disagrees with the draft model at any point in the sequence, it identifies the first mismatch. The system then accepts all tokens up to that point and regenerates the remaining sequence starting from the mismatched token. This ensures that the final output is identical to what the target model would have produced if it had generated the text token by token from the beginning. The draft model’s role is purely to guess ahead; the target model acts as the ground truth, ensuring accuracy.

This method does not change the underlying logic or the final text produced by the primary model. It simply optimizes the computational path. By batching the verification of multiple tokens, speculative decoding reduces the number of times the slower, more resource-intensive target model needs to perform a full forward pass. The speedup comes from parallelizing the draft generation and minimizing the number of sequential steps required for the target model. As long as the draft model is sufficiently aligned with the target model, the overhead of verification is low, and the overall generation time is significantly reduced without sacrificing the quality or content of the output.

Think of it this way. Normally, to generate ten words, the large model has to do ten separate forward passes—one per word—because each new word depends on all the previous ones. That sequential chaining is what makes text generation slow, no matter how powerful the model is.

Speculative decoding attacks that bottleneck with two models working together. First, a small, fast "draft" model quickly proposes a short sequence of the next tokens, say four or eight of them at a time. It's a best guess, a rough sketch of what you think the large model is about to say. Then—and this is the crucial part—you feed that entire proposed sequence into the large model in a single forward pass. Because a transformer processes all input tokens in parallel, the large model can verify the whole batch in one shot rather than token by token. It essentially asks, "For each of these positions, would I have generated this token, or something else?"

If every proposed token matches what the large model would actually output, you keep the entire batch and move on to the next speculative round. If there's a mismatch at some position, say the fourth token is off, you keep the first three, let the large model generate its own correct fourth token, and then restart the speculative cycle from that corrected point.

The output is identical to what the large model would have produced on its own because the large model is the one doing the final verification at every step. The draft model only ever proposes; it never gets a say in what ultimately ends up in your text. You can think of it as a student writing out the next ten lines of an essay while the professor reads them all at once and only corrects the first line that's wrong.

The speedup scales with how often the small model guesses correctly. If the proposed tokens are usually all correct, you've cut your number of large-model forward passes by a factor of four or eight. If the draft model is bad and keeps disagreeing early on, you gain almost nothing. But for most natural text and with a sufficiently similar small model, the agreement rate is high enough that you get a real, tangible reduction in generation time without any change to the quality or content of what you get back.

plain.content:
When you insert a key-value pair into a hash map, the map first runs that key through a hash function to get an integer, which it then uses (typically via a modulo operation) to determine a bucket index in an internal array. The problem is that two different keys can produce the same index, especially once the number of stored entries grows relative to the size of that array. This is a collision, and the map must decide how to store both entries. The most common strategy is separate chaining, in which each bucket in the array doesn't hold a single pair but instead references a linked list (or some equivalent linked structure) of all entries that hash to that index. On a collision, the new pair is simply appended to that bucket's list. Lookup then becomes a two-step process: compute the index to find the correct bucket, then scan through that bucket's chain until the matching key is located. The alternative strategy is open addressing, where instead of using a secondary structure per bucket, the map probes the array itself—checking the next index, then the next, and so on (using some stride pattern like linear, quadratic, or double hashing) until it finds an empty slot. Both approaches work, but chaining is more common in many language standard library implementations because it keeps the array structure simple and avoids the awkwardness of a nearly-full array with few open slots.

As to when the map resizes, the trigger is the load factor, which is essentially the ratio of the number of stored entries to the capacity of the underlying array. If the load factor exceeds a threshold the implementation chose (commonly around 0.75 to 1.0, depending on the language and its specific design), the map allocates a new, larger internal array—typically double the previous size—and rehashes every key into its position in the new array. This is necessary because without it, in the chaining case, the average length of the chains grows, which degrades lookup performance from constant time toward something closer to linear in the number of elements in a bucket. In the open addressing case, the situation is more severe because a high load factor means many probe sequences are long before finding an empty slot, and if the array ever becomes completely full, an insertion can cycle forever with no empty slot to find. So resizes are almost always triggered preemptively, well before the array is full. The resize operation itself is where most of the constant-factor cost of hash map insertions comes from, because every single key must be rehashed and relocated, making it an O(n) operation. But because it happens relatively infrequently—only logarithmically often over the lifetime of the map, since doubling the capacity each time means the number of resizes needed to store n elements is O(log n)—the amortized cost across many insertions remains constant, keeping the overall average-case performance of hash map operations at O(1).

Here is the core idea, stripped of the jargon:

When a large language model generates text normally, it writes one token at a time. Each new token depends on all the previous ones, so you cannot start computing the third token until the second is finished. This serial process is slow, even though much of the GPU is sitting idle during each step.

Speculative decoding attacks that bottleneck with a simple two-model trick. First, you have a small, fast model—a "draft" model—that makes a rapid guess of what a short sequence of tokens the large model would actually produce. Because it is small, it can generate, say, six tokens in the time the large model would take to produce one.

Then the large model does not generate those six tokens sequentially. Instead, it receives all six candidate tokens at once and checks them in a single parallel step. This is the crucial efficiency win: the expensive model has been forced to work serially, but now it is doing one forward pass over six positions instead of six sequential one-position passes.

The large model then decides, token by token, whether each draft token is correct. It accepts every token it agrees with. At the first position where it disagrees, it stops, keeps everything accepted so far, and continues from that point on its own (or by requesting a new draft from the small model). The large model's decision rule is unchanged from normal generation, so the final output is exactly what the large model would have produced on its own. The small model never gets to commit a token; it only proposes, and the large model always has the final say.

This means you get a speedup that can be substantial, especially in contexts where the small model has a high probability of being right, without changing the quality or content of the output at all. The only thing that changes is the scheduling: you have traded a sequence of short, slow serial steps for one fast guess followed by one fast parallel verification, and the large model's role is identical in both cases.

plain.content:
When two different keys produce the same hash value when you run them through a hash function, you've hit a collision. The hash function has tried to map each key to a unique bucket in an underlying array, but the math simply didn't work out that time. The hash map has to deal with the fact that more than one key is now claiming the same slot, and the most common strategies fall into two broad categories.

The first and perhaps most traditional approach is called chaining. Each bucket in the array doesn't hold just a single key-value pair. Instead, it holds a pointer to a linked list (or in some implementations, a small dynamic array) of all the entries that happened to hash to that particular index. So if three different keys all end up at index 7, index 7's bucket simply holds a little linked list containing all three, and you walk down the list when looking up a value. Insertion is a matter of appending to that list, deletion means finding and removing the right node, and the cost of a lookup degrades only if a particular bucket accumulates a lot of entries. In well-designed situations with a reasonable load factor, these lists tend to stay short, so the overhead is minimal.

The second broad approach is open addressing. Here the array is a flat set of slots with no per-slot list. When you hit a collision, instead of moving to a separate list, you probe the array itself to find the next available slot. Simplest variant, linear probing, just checks the next index, then the next one after that, wrapping around at the end of the array, until you find a free cell. Quadratic probing and double hashing follow similar logic but generate their probe sequence in a way that spreads out the lookups and reduces clustering. The trade-off here is that all entries live directly in the array, which is cache-friendly, but a full slot can make probing take multiple steps, and deletion is slightly trickier because you can't just set a slot to "empty" without potentially breaking the probe chain for later lookups (which is why tombstone markers are often used).

Now, when does the map need to resize? Both strategies suffer when too many keys are crammed into too few slots. For chaining, once a bucket's list gets long, every lookup at that bucket is degrading from constant-time to linear-in-list-length. For open addressing, once the array fills past a certain density, probing chains get long and lookups can actually start taking proportional time to the number of elements, and at 100 percent occupancy you can never insert a new element. The standard safeguard is a threshold called the load factor, which is simply the ratio of actual number of elements to the capacity of the array. In most mainstream implementations (Java's HashMap, for instance), the trigger is a load factor of 0.75. The moment you insert an element and the ratio of element count to array length exceeds that threshold, the map is told it's time to grow.

Resizing works as follows. The map allocates a new internal array whose size is typically a power of two and at least double the old one. It then takes every existing key-value pair, recomputes its hash modulo the new length (so the bucket index may change entirely), and reinserts it into the fresh structure. For a chained map, each element is re-placed into whatever bucket its hash now lands in. For an open-addressing map, each element is re-probed until it finds a valid slot. After all old elements are settled, the reference to the new structure is swapped in and the old one is discarded. This is an O(n) operation, but because it only happens geometrically less and less often as the map grows, the amortized cost of any single insertion remains constant. In other words, you pay a brief, infrequent reorganization cost to keep the everyday operations fast.

Some implementations, notably Java's HashMap since version 8, introduce a hybrid optimization: when a single bucket's collision list grows beyond roughly eight nodes, those entries are converted into a small balanced binary search tree (a red-black tree internally). This means that even in the pathological worst case where many keys hash to the same bucket, lookups stay at O(log n) rather than O(n), which is a meaningful guarantee against adversarial or just-bad-input scenarios. But for normal usage with a reasonable distribution, the list is short, the tree conversion is rare, and the map behaves as the textbook description suggests.

Its weights are untouched, and its probability distribution over every possible continuation of the text is identical to what it would have produced had you simply asked it to generate token by token with no help. You have only changed the order in which those computations happen. The draft model may be wrong, and when it is, the large model simply catches the error and corrects it, exactly as it would have if it were generating that token on its own. A hash map works by taking a key, running it through a hash function, and using the numerical result to index into a fixed-size array of buckets. The problem is that two different keys can produce the same hash value, and in that case both keys want to land in the same bucket. This is a collision, and it's not just a theoretical edge case — for any non-trivial set of keys, it's a matter of when and not if, it will happen.

There are two principal strategies for dealing with a given collision, and most languages commit to one or the other. With open addressing, the hash map doesn't attach multiple keys to the same bucket at all. Instead, when you probe and find the bucket already occupied, the algorithm simply moves to the next bucket — using some deterministic stride or secondary hashing — until it finds an empty slot or a slot occupied by a key that truly belongs there. The array itself stays dense; there's no visible "extra" data attached to any single index. With chaining, or separate chaining, each bucket holds not a single key but a small linked list (or similar structure) of keys that all hash to that index. When a new key arrives and the bucket is non-empty, it's simply appended to that list. Lookups then involve computing the hash to find the right bucket, then walking through the small list until the matching key is found. Chaining tends to be more common in practice in many standard library implementations, while open addressing is used in others and is often favored for its cache-friendliness.

Resizing, or rehashing, is the process of the map deciding that its current array has grown too crowded and needs a larger one to maintain its performance guarantees. The trigger is almost always a measure of how "full" the map has become, known as the load factor. This is typically calculated as the ratio of the number of stored entries to the number of available buckets. Once that ratio exceeds some predefined threshold — commonly around 0.75 in many implementations — the map knows that lookups are starting to degrade, either because chains in separate-chaining mode are getting long or because probes in open-addressing mode are having to traverse many already-occupied slots before finding a free one.

When the decision to resize is made, the map allocates a new internal array, usually at roughly twice the size of the old one (or the next prime number of appropriate magnitude, in the case of open-addressing, to preserve good distribution properties). It then takes every single entry currently in the old structure, recomputes its hash, and determines which bucket in the newly sized array it should now inhabit. Because the bucket count has changed, many keys will end up in different positions than before, which is why a full rehash is necessary rather than just inserting the new key into the existing structure. All references from outside the map continue to work because the map itself manages the internal bookkeeping, but the operation has a cost proportional to the total number of entries, which is why the threshold is set so that this full rebuild happens infrequently, spread out across many individual insertions.

When two different keys happen to hash to the same index in a hash map's underlying array, a collision occurs. There are two main strategies for dealing with this situation, and most common implementations pick one of them. The first, known as chaining, involves attaching a small linked list (or sometimes a balanced tree in languages like Java's HashMap) at each array slot. When a collision is detected, the new key-value pair is simply appended to that existing list, so multiple entries can live at the same index. The second approach, called open addressing, keeps everything within the array itself. If a target slot is already occupied, the map probes outward—checking the next slot, or the next slot after that, or some other deterministic sequence dictated by a secondary hash function—until it finds a free space to place the value. A hash map tracks a metric called the load factor, which is essentially the ratio of stored entries to available slots in the array. Once that ratio crosses a predefined threshold—often around 0.75 in common implementations like Java's HashMap, or sometimes even 0.5—triggering a resize makes it statistically likely that collision chains or probe sequences are growing long enough to noticeably slow down lookups, insertions, and deletions. At that point, the map allocates a new internal array, typically with double the previous capacity. Every existing key-value pair is then iterated over, rehashed against the larger array's dimension, and reinserted at its new computed index. This rehashing step is what actually makes resizing expensive; it is an O(n) operation, where n is the total number of entries, because every single element must be touched again. That is why the map waits until the load factor genuinely demands it rather than growing more aggressively, balancing memory against performance. After resizing, the load factor drops back down to a low value, giving the map room to grow before it will ever need to rehash again.

In practice, what the user experiences is that most operations on a hash map—lookup, insertion, deletion—remain constant time on average. The occasional rehash is a one-time cost that gets amortized across all the subsequent cheap operations that happen before the next threshold is hit. If you were to insert millions of distinct keys all at once into a new empty map, you would see the resize happen a few times over the course of that insertion burst, but the cost of each resize is proportional to the size at that moment, so it does not create a pathological slowdown for the work that follows.

When two different keys end up producing the same hash value, or more precisely the same array index after that hash is reduced, you've hit a collision. There are fundamentally two strategies for dealing with this. The first is called separate chaining. With that approach, each slot in the underlying array holds not a single key-value pair but rather a whole linked list of pairs. When a collision occurs, the new entry is simply appended to the head of that chain, so the two keys coexist in the same bucket. Lookup still works by first computing the hash to find the right slot, then walking down that particular list comparing keys until you find the one you need. In the common case where no collision has happened, the list has just one element and you're done immediately; in the worst case where everything hashed to the same slot, you'd end up scanning an entire list. The second strategy, called open addressing (with sub-variants like linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing), is different. There are no separate lists. Instead, when the computed slot is already occupied, the hash function is slightly modified—usually by adding a small increment to the index, wrapping around if you reach the end—and you try the next slot. You keep stepping through the array until you find an empty slot where you can store your entry. This keeps all your data in one flat array, which plays nicely with CPU cache, but it does mean you have to leave some slots deliberately empty, or the probe sequence can't distinguish between "this slot is the one for my key" and "this slot was just passed through during a previous collision."

As for when the map decides to resize itself, the trigger is almost always a measure of how full the table has become, most commonly referred to as the load factor. That is simply the ratio of the number of stored entries to the number of available slots in the array. Once that ratio exceeds some threshold—typically around 0.75 for implementations like Java's HashMap or Python's CPython dict—the structure determines that performance is starting to degrade. Under separate chaining, longer and longer lists mean lookups are shifting from O(1) toward O(n). Under open addressing, as the table gets fuller, probe sequences get longer because you keep bumping into occupied slots before finding a free one. At some point the performance drop-off becomes too steep to tolerate, so the structure preemptively acts before things get that bad.

When resizing is actually triggered, the map allocates a new internal array that is larger than the old one. The growth is almost always multiplicative rather than additive—you double the capacity rather than adding a fixed number—because you want to keep the load factor in a healthy range after reinsertion. Then, and this is the costly part, every single existing entry in the old array has to be rehashed against the new array's size. Because the array's length has changed, every key will in general land in a different index, so you can't just copy the old array over; you have to compute a fresh bucket position for each element and place it accordingly. During this rehashing, the structure is typically in a somewhat transitional state, and depending on the implementation it may process one element at a time (which means concurrent accesses are handled carefully, for instance through internal locking or by building the new table entirely and then swapping pointers atomically) or it may rehash in batches. In a properly synchronized or thread-safe implementation the whole operation is atomic from the outside; in a non-synchronized one you just don't resize while another thread is mid-lookup, or you use a design that tolerates the intermediate state.

It's also worth noting that shrinking is far rarer than growing. Some implementations will shrink the table when the load factor drops well below a lower threshold, say after a series of removals, but this is sometimes omitted entirely or done only when the table has been reduced by a significant number of entries, because the cost of a full rehash on every tiny change is rarely worth the memory savings. The net effect is that a hash map will grow its internal table as needed to keep its average performance close to constant-time per operation, paying the occasional O(n) cost of a full rehash to amortize that over many subsequent O(1) operations.

When you insert an item into a hash map, the system takes your key, runs it through a hash function, and gets back an integer that determines which bucket or array slot the item goes into. The first approach is called chaining, where each bucket holds not a single item but a small collection—typically a linked list or, in many modern implementations, a short contiguous array of pointers. When you insert an item, you hash the key to find the right bucket, and then you simply append the item to whatever list is already there. To look up a key later, you hash it to find the bucket, then walk through the list inside that bucket comparing keys until you find a match or run out. The cost of a collision here is small: you only have to compare against the other items that also landed in that specific bucket rather than the whole map.

The second strategy is open addressing. Here the map uses a single flat array with no lists at all. When a collision occurs, the map simply probes to the next slot in the array using some predetermined pattern—linear probing means checking the very next index, quadratic probing means checking offset by a multiple of the probe number, or in some cases a completely different random-looking sequence. The reason this rehashing step exists is that even though the capacity has grown, the old hash function still maps every key into a space that was only as wide as the old array.
